sentences.nl: Vandaag oefenen we Nederlandse zinnen, met de grammatica van #dutchgrammar les 29, over het modale werkwoord ‘zullen’.
sentences.en: Today we are practicing Dutch sentences, with the grammar from #dutchgrammar lesson 29, about the modal verb 'zullen'.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Today practice we Dutch sentences, with the grammar of #dutchgrammar lesson 29, about the modal verb 'shall'.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Vandaag oefenen we" follows the common Dutch sentence structure of [Time - Verb - Subject].  
• "met de grammatica van" uses "met" (with) to indicate involvement or accompaniment, and "van" (of) to show possession.  
• "het modale werkwoord 'zullen'" uses the definite article "het" for singular neuter nouns, and "modale werkwoord" refers to the category of modal verbs.

– "Morgen leren we nieuwe woorden." (Tomorrow we learn new words.)  
– "We praten over de les van gisteren." (We talk about the lesson of yesterday.)  
– "Hij zal de grammatica begrijpen." (He shall understand the grammar.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Morgen bespreken we de oefeningen, met de hulp van onze leraar. (Tomorrow we will discuss the exercises, with the help of our teacher.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch education, grammar lessons are often numbered and categorized, as seen in "#dutchgrammar les 29", reflecting a structured approach to language learning.

sentences.nl: ‘Ja’, zegt Lars,, hier zul je wel goed kunnen studeren.
sentences.en: "Yes," says Lars, "you'll be able to study well here."
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• "Yes," says Lars, "here will you surely well be able to study."

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Word Order**: The sentence uses inversion with "zegt Lars" to introduce direct speech, which is common in Dutch.  
• **Modal Verb 'kunnen'**: The verb "kunnen" (to be able to) is used here, and it is placed at the end of the clause following "zullen" (will).  
• **'Wel' Usage**: "Wel" is used here to add emphasis or certainty, often translated as "surely" or "indeed".  

Examples:  
  - Morgen zul je wel vroeg opstaan. (Tomorrow you will surely get up early.)  
  - Hier kun je wel lekker eten. (Here, you can surely eat well.)  
  - Dit boek zul je wel leuk vinden. (You will surely like this book.)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Daar zul je wel veel plezier hebben." (There you will surely have a lot of fun.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In the Netherlands, education is highly valued, and there is a strong emphasis on finding a conducive environment for studying. This sentence reflects the importance placed on having a good study environment.

• I recognize your voice from the videos.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Ik herken je stem" uses the verb "herkennen," which means "to recognize." The direct object "je stem" (your voice) follows the verb.  
• "Van de filmpjes" uses the preposition "van" to indicate origin or source, meaning "from the videos."  
• Example 1: "Ik herken zijn gezicht van de foto." (I recognize his face from the photo.)  
• Example 2: "Ze herkennen dat liedje van de radio." (They recognize that song from the radio.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Ik herken die plek van onze vakantie." (I recognize that place from our vacation.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In the Netherlands, many people consume a wide variety of videos online, from educational content to entertainment, which makes recognizing voices from videos a common experience.

• The adjective "aangenaam" can be used more broadly to describe things that are enjoyable or agreeable.

sentences.nl: Het zal vanavond ook nog wel mooi weer zijn.
sentences.en: The weather will probably be nice tonight as well.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• It will this evening also still indeed nice weather be.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Het zal" is the future tense formed by "zal" (will) and refers to "it".  
• "Vanavond" means "this evening" and is an adverb of time.  
• "Ook nog wel" is a combination of words meaning "also still indeed", adding emphasis or expectation.  
• "Mooi weer" translates to "nice weather", a common phrase for pleasant weather conditions.  
• Dutch sentences often place time expressions early in the sentence.

• Extra Phrases:  
  - "Het zal morgen ook wel druk zijn." (It will probably be busy tomorrow too.)  
  - "Zij zal vanavond nog wel bellen." (She will probably call this evening.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Het zal waarschijnlijk ook een lange dag worden." (It will probably be a long day as well.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• Discussing the weather is a common topic in Dutch social interaction, often used as a conversation starter. The phrase "mooi weer" is frequently used in both casual and formal settings.

sentences.nl: Je betaalt voor de les en de accommodatie.
sentences.en: You pay for the lesson and the accommodation.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• You pay for the lesson and the accommodation.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Je betaalt" is in the present tense, meaning "you pay." The verb "betalen" is conjugated for the second-person singular.  
• "voor" is a preposition meaning "for," used to indicate the purpose or recipient of an action.  
• "de les" and "de accommodatie" are both nouns with the definite article "de," indicating specific objects. Dutch uses "de" or "het" as definite articles, "de" is for common gender nouns.  
• Example sentences:  
  - "Je betaalt voor de koffie." (You pay for the coffee.)  
  - "Hij betaalt voor het kaartje." (He pays for the ticket.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Hij betaalt voor het diner en de drankjes. (He pays for the dinner and the drinks.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In the Netherlands, it is common to pay separately or "split the bill" when dining out, known as "pinnen" or "tikkie" in casual settings.

sentences.nl: Maar al het andere doen we samen…

sentences.nl: Hoe zullen we het organiseren?
sentences.en: How shall we organize it?
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• How shall we it organize?

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• The sentence starts with "Hoe" (How), which is a common way to begin a question in Dutch.  
• "Zullen" is an auxiliary verb used for forming the future tense or to suggest a possibility or offer, similar to "shall" in English.  
• The structure "zullen we" implies a suggestion or a plan.  
• The word order is inverted for a question: Verb-Subject-Object (VS(O)).  
• Example sentences:  
  - "Hoe zullen we dat aanpakken?" (How shall we tackle that?)  
  - "Wanneer zullen we vertrekken?" (When shall we leave?)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Hoe zullen we de taken verdelen?" (How shall we divide the tasks?)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch-speaking cultures, discussing plans or organizing events often involves collaborative decision-making, which is reflected in the use of "zullen we" to suggest joint decisions.

sentences.nl: Iedereen kan iets doen:, naar de winkel,, geld inzamelen bij de andere studenten, salades maken
sentences.en: Everyone can do something: go to the store, collect money from the other students, make salads.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Everyone can something do: to the store, money collect at the other students, salads make.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• The sentence lists various activities with commas, showing a range of actions people can take.  
• "Iedereen kan iets doen" (Everyone can do something) uses the modal verb "kan" (can) followed by an infinitive, a common structure to express ability.  
• "Inzamelen" (collect) is a separable verb. In a sentence, it can be split: "Wij zamelen geld in" (We collect money).  
• Examples:  
  - Iedereen kan helpen met het opruimen. (Everyone can help with cleaning up.)  
  - Zij kan goed zingen op het podium. (She can sing well on stage.)  
  - We kunnen samen geld inzamelen voor het goede doel. (We can collect money together for charity.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Iedereen kan bijdragen aan het project: ideeën geven, onderzoek doen, presentaties voorbereiden. (Everyone can contribute to the project: give ideas, do research, prepare presentations.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• Volunteering and community involvement are common in Dutch culture, often reflected in activities like fundraising or organizing events.

sentences.nl: de barbecue aansteken,, het vlees braden, en opruimen op het einde.
sentences.en: Light the barbecue, roast the meat, and clean up at the end.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• the barbecue light, the meat roast, and clean up at the end.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• This sentence uses a sequence of infinitives: "aansteken," "braden," and "opruimen." In Dutch, infinitives can be used to list actions without specifying a subject explicitly.  
• "Op het einde" translates to "at the end," a common way to indicate the conclusion of an event or series of actions.  
• Examples:  
  - "De auto wassen, de banden oppompen, en de olie verversen." (Wash the car, pump up the tires, and change the oil.)  
  - "De kamer schoonmaken, de planten water geven, en de deuren sluiten." (Clean the room, water the plants, and close the doors.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• De computer aanzetten, de e-mails lezen, en afsluiten aan het einde. (Turn on the computer, read the emails, and shut down at the end.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In the Netherlands, barbecuing is a popular activity during the summer months, often seen as a social event where friends and family gather. It’s common to have everyone participate in various tasks such as lighting the barbecue, cooking, and cleaning up.

sentences.nl: Dan zullen wij het hier regelen, met de andere studenten.
sentences.en: Then we will arrange it here, with the other students.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Then will we it here arrange, with the other students.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Dan" is used to indicate a future time, often translated as "then" in English.  
• The verb "zullen" is used for future tense or to indicate a strong intention, similar to "will" in English.  
• "Regelen" means "to arrange" or "to organize."  
• "Met de andere studenten" means "with the other students," showing the use of "met" for "with."

Extra phrases/sentences:  
• "Dan gaan we naar het park." (Then we will go to the park.)  
• "Wij zullen het morgen regelen." (We will arrange it tomorrow.)  
• "Met de andere leraren bespreken we het plan." (With the other teachers, we discuss the plan.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Morgen zullen wij de presentatie voorbereiden, samen met de collega's. (Tomorrow we will prepare the presentation, together with the colleagues.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch educational settings, group projects and collaboration are common, so arranging tasks with other students is a frequent activity.

sentences.nl: Voor hoeveel zullen we eten kopen? — Voor hoeveel studenten? — Vandaag komen 25 studenten.
sentences.en: For how much will we buy food? — For how many students? — Today 25 students are coming.

sentences.nl: Ik bedoel het budget per persoon.
sentences.en: I mean the budget per person.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Ik bedoel het budget per persoon.  
(I mean the budget per person.)

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Ik bedoel" is the first person singular form of the verb "bedoelen," meaning "to mean" or "to refer to."  
• "Het budget" is a noun phrase meaning "the budget." Dutch uses "het" as the definite article for neuter nouns.  
• "Per persoon" is a prepositional phrase meaning "per person." "Per" is used similarly in Dutch and English to indicate distribution or ratio.  

• Examples:  
  - "Ik bedoel de tijd per sessie." (I mean the time per session.)  
  - "We bespreken het schema per afdeling." (We discuss the schedule per department.)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Ik bedoel de kosten per item." (I mean the costs per item.)

sentences.nl: Wij kunnen met 2 personen, niet voor 25 mensen eten meenemen op de fiets.
sentences.en: We can take food for 2 people, not for 25 people, on the bike.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• We can with 2 people, not for 25 people food take on the bike.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Wij kunnen" means "we can," indicating ability or permission.  
• "met 2 personen" uses "met" (with) to indicate inclusion or accompaniment.  
• "niet voor 25 mensen" uses "voor" (for) to indicate purpose or intended recipients, and "niet" (not) to negate the capability.  
• "eten meenemen" translates to "take food," where "meenemen" (to take/bring along) is a separable verb.  
• "op de fiets" uses "op" (on) to indicate the mode of transport.

• Extra phrases:  
  - "Ik kan met mijn vriend naar de bioscoop gaan." (I can go to the cinema with my friend.)  
  - "Zij wil niet voor iedereen koken." (She doesn't want to cook for everyone.)  
  - "Wij nemen onze boeken mee naar school." (We take our books to school.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Wij kunnen met drie mensen, niet voor 30 gasten een feest organiseren." (We can organize a party with three people, not for 30 guests.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In the Netherlands, cycling is a very common mode of transport. People often use bikes to carry groceries or other goods, sometimes even in large quantities. However, there are practical limits to how much one can transport by bike.

sentences.nl: Ik zal de drank kopen.
sentences.en: I will buy the drinks.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• I will the drink buy.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• The sentence uses the future tense with "zal" (will) followed by the infinitive verb "kopen" (to buy). The structure is: Subject + "zal" + Object + Infinitive Verb.  
• "De drank" means "the drink". "De" is the definite article used for common gender nouns in Dutch.  
• Example Sentences:  
  - "Hij zal het boek lezen." (He will read the book.)  
  - "Zij zal de auto wassen." (She will wash the car.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Wij zullen de taart bakken." (We will bake the cake.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch culture, offering to buy drinks can be a friendly gesture, often seen in social gatherings or when meeting friends at a café or bar.

sentences.nl: Dat is een beetje zwaar op de fiets.
sentences.en: That is a bit heavy on the bike.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• That is a bit heavy on the bike.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Dat is" (That is) is a simple present tense construction used for stating facts or opinions.  
• "Een beetje" (a bit) is a common phrase used to describe a small amount or degree.  
• "Zwaar" (heavy) is an adjective describing weight or difficulty.  
• "Op de fiets" (on the bike) indicates the method or means of transportation, using "op" (on) as a preposition.

Extra phrases:  
• "Dat is een beetje moeilijk." (That is a bit difficult.)  
• "Hij is een beetje moe." (He is a bit tired.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Dat is een beetje koud voor een zomerdag." (That is a bit cold for a summer day.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• Biking is a common mode of transportation in the Netherlands, with dedicated bike lanes and infrastructure, making phrases related to cycling frequently used in everyday conversation.

sentences.nl: En met mij kunnen ook nog mensen meerijden.
sentences.en: And with me, other people can also ride along.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• And with me can also still people ride-along.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• The sentence uses inversion, a common structure in Dutch where the verb comes before the subject, after an introductory element ("En met mij").  
• "Meerijden" is a separable verb: "mee" (along) and "rijden" (to ride). In the infinitive form, they stay together.  
• "Ook nog" means "also still" and emphasizes inclusivity or additional capacity.

Extra Sentences:  
• Morgen kan ik ook nog komen. (Tomorrow I can also still come.)  
• Zij wil met ons meerijden. (She wants to ride along with us.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Met de trein kunnen we ook nog reizen. (With the train, we can also still travel.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In the Netherlands, carpooling is quite common due to environmental awareness and practicality, especially for commuting. "Meerijden" reflects a collaborative transport culture.

nederlands.spelling: The 'ee' in 'nee' is a long vowel /eː/ and the 'a' in 'lands' is a short vowel /ɑ/.
nederlands.fast: In rapid speech, the final /ts/ in 'nederlands' may be reduced, causing it to blend with following words.

dit.spelling: The short vowel /ɪ/ is followed by a voiceless plosive /t/, typical of closed syllables.
dit.fast: In rapid speech, the /t/ in ‘dit is’ can become a flap [ɾ] or be elided entirely.

een.spelling: The article ‘een’ is pronounced with a long /eː/ to distinguish it from the numeral ‘één’, which has a stressed pronunciation.
een.fast: In rapid speech, ‘een’ may be reduced to a schwa sound /ən/ when it is unstressed.

aflevering.spelling: The prefix ‘af-’ indicates a separable prefix, showing a clear boundary with the root.
aflevering.fast: The initial /f/ of ‘aflevering’ may assimilate to a voiced [v] in connected speech, especially after voiced sounds.

van.spelling: The short vowel /ɑ/ is common in monosyllabic words ending in -n.
van.fast: The final /n/ in ‘van’ is often elided in casual speech, particularly before consonants.

heb.spelling: Heb is a monosyllabic word with a short vowel /ɛ/ followed by a voiced bilabial plosive /b/.
heb.fast: In rapid speech, the final /b/ in ‘heb ik’ might be pronounced as a flap or even omitted entirely before the following vowel.

zin.fast: In rapid speech, the final /n/ in ‘zin heb’ may be realized as a nasalized vowel or dropped in informal contexts.

vandaag.spelling: The combination 'aa' in 'vandaag' indicates a long /aː/ sound, typical for Dutch vowels.
vandaag.fast: The final /x/ in 'vandaag' may be softened or dropped in rapid speech, especially if followed by a vowel.

oefenen.spelling: The sequence 'oe' represents a long /uː/ sound.
oefenen.fast: In casual speech, the final /n/ in ‘oefenen’ may be fully assimilated or nasalized before a vowel.

grammatica.spelling: The initial gr- and -a- in 'grammatica' follow the usual Dutch pronunciation rules for similar Greek-origin words.
grammatica.fast: In rapid speech, the final /a/ in 'grammatica' may be pronounced as a schwa [ə] when followed by a word starting with a consonant.

dutchgrammar.fast: In connected speech, the final /r/ in ‘grammar’ may become less pronounced or vocalized.

les.spelling: Short /ɛ/ in a closed syllable followed by a voiceless /s/.
les.fast: In rapid speech, the final /s/ in ‘les is’ may become voiceless between vowels, leading to a pronunciation like [lɛsɪs].

over.spelling: The open syllable 'o-' shows the long /oː/ vowel.
over.fast: In connected speech, final /r/ in 'over' may be pronounced as a flap or even omitted depending on regional accents.

het.spelling: The ‘h’ is often silent in casual speech, making it sound like ‘et’.
het.fast: In rapid speech, the initial /h/ in ‘het’ may be elided, resulting in a pronunciation closer to [ɛt].

naar.spelling: The long vowel /aː/ appears in the open syllable with the consonant ending.
naar.fast: The final /r/ in ‘naar’ can often be a tapped [ɾ] or even silent in casual speech when followed by a word starting with a consonant.

wat.spelling: The short vowel /ɑ/ is common in closed syllables.
wat.fast: In connected speech, 'wat' often reduces to /wət/ or even /wə/ before vowels.

anika.spelling: The open vowel 'a' in the first syllable is long, indicated by the IPA /aː/.
anika.fast: The final /a/ in 'anika' can be pronounced with a shorter, more central vowel sound in rapid speech.

wel.spelling: The short vowel /ɛ/ is pronounced because the syllable is closed by the consonant /l/.
wel.fast: In connected speech, the /l/ in ‘wel ik’ might become a dark [ɫ] before a vowel.

welkom.spelling: The combination 'w' and 'e' produces a /ʋɛ/ sound, common in Dutch words starting with 'wel-'.
welkom.fast: In fast speech, the final /m/ in 'welkom' can become nasalized before a following vowel.

bij.spelling: The diphthong /ɛi̯/ is common in Dutch, often spelled with 'ij'.
bij.fast: In fast speech, the diphthong /ɛi̯/ in 'bij' might be slightly reduced, blending smoothly into following words.

ben.spelling: Short vowel /ɛ/ in closed syllable with nasal ending.
ben.fast: In rapid speech, 'ben ik' may sound like [bɛnɪk] with reduced vowel.

nog.spelling: The word 'nog' ends in a voiced velar fricative /x/, which is common in Dutch adverbs.
nog.fast: In rapid speech, the final /x/ in ‘nog’ may be devoiced or slightly reduced before a vowel.

ook.spelling: The long vowel /oː/ is indicated by the open syllable followed by a consonant.
ook.fast: In casual speech, the vowel /oː/ can sometimes become shorter before a following consonant.

zijn.spelling: The diphthong 'ij' in 'zijn' is pronounced as /ɛi/.
zijn.fast: In fast speech, 'zijn' may reduce to a schwa sound, especially in unstressed positions.

dan.spelling: Short vowel /ɑ/ in closed syllable, typical for monosyllabic adverbs.
